title: Reading What the Compiler Tells You

questions.question: A build produces six errors. How many mistakes are in the file?
options: There is no way to tell without reading all of them
At least six
Fewer than six, and possibly one, because the compiler carries on after a mistake and reports what follows against a misunderstanding
Exactly six
questions.explanation: Measured in this lesson: four mistakes produce six errors on both GCC and Clang, and fixing the first removes three of them.

questions.question: Three errors say a name is not a member of std. What is the most likely cause?
options: The wrong C++ standard was selected
Three different names spelled wrongly
The standard library is not installed
One missing include, used in three places
questions.explanation: The standard library is a set of headers rather than one thing you get automatically, and a header is usually used more than once, which is why this produces the most errors per line of cause.

questions.question: What is on the note: lines under an error?
options: Information for compiler authors
Extra warnings that can be ignored
A repeat of the error in different words
Frequently the answer, such as which header to include or where a function was declared
questions.explanation: GCC will print the exact include you forgot. The line gets skipped constantly because it does not say error and sits in the middle of a wall of text.

questions.question: The compiler says a semicolon is expected, and the line it names looks correct. Where is the mistake?
options: Always on the line named
At the caret, or in the statement above it, which did not end
In a header, since the file itself is fine
Always exactly one line above
questions.explanation: Measured on GCC 11 and Clang 14, three cases in four now name the right line and print the missing character under a caret. The one that still lands late on GCC is a declaration whose next line starts another declaration.

questions.question: You have twelve errors. Which do you fix first?
options: The last one, since it is the most recent
All the ones that mention the same file
The first one, then rebuild before reading anything else
The easiest looking one, to reduce the count
questions.explanation: The easy looking ones near the bottom are the most likely to be consequences of the hard looking one at the top, so fixing them is often work on a problem that does not exist.

questions.question: Every error names a header from the standard library that you have never opened. What now?
options: Scroll up to the in file included from line, which names the line of yours that started it
Report a bug against the standard library
Reinstall the compiler
Delete the include and write the code yourself
questions.explanation: Errors reported inside a header are almost always caused by the file that included it. See E-CPP-0003.
